channel.title: Kotsu
channel.description: A Japanese orthopedic surgeon checks what the research actually says about staying strong, mobile and young — muscles, bones, joints, connective tissue, skin and hair.

item.title: Does shoulder impingement surgery work? What the placebo-surgery trials show
item.description: Arthroscopic subacromial decompression — 'shaving the bone' for shoulder impingement — was one of the most common shoulder operations. A surgeon reads the two trials that compared it with placebo surgery, one followed for ten years, and the reviews and guideline that came after.

item.title: Does a cortisone shot help tennis elbow? What the trials show
item.description: A steroid injection is one of the most common treatments for tennis elbow. A surgeon reads the randomised trials that followed people for a year — including one with a placebo injection — to see what the shot does in the first weeks, and what it does after that.

item.title: Does a knee brace help knee arthritis? What the trials show
item.description: Knee braces are one of the most common things people try for an arthritic knee. A surgeon reads a Cochrane review, two meta-analyses of unloader-brace trials that disagree, and the main guidelines to see what a brace can and can't do.

item.title: Should you rest and ice a sprained ankle? RICE, checked
item.description: Rest, ice, compression, elevation: almost everyone knows the RICE rule for a twisted ankle. A surgeon reads the reviews of RICE and ice trials, an overview of 46 systematic reviews, and a meta-analysis of rehabilitation exercise to see what actually helps a sprained ankle recover.

item.title: Does bending your back when you lift cause back pain? 'Lift with your legs', checked
item.description: Almost everyone has been told to keep their back straight and lift with their legs. A surgeon reads a meta-analysis of lifting posture and back pain, a Cochrane review of lifting-technique training in more than 20,000 workers, and a meta-analysis of what actually prevents back pain.

item.title: Does losing weight take pressure off arthritic knees? The '4 pounds' claim, checked
item.description: You may have heard that every pound you lose takes four pounds off your knees. A surgeon reads the gait study behind that number, two randomised trials of diet and exercise in 1,277 people with knee arthritis, and a meta-analysis, to see what weight loss really does for knee pain.

item.title: Is walking bad for knee arthritis? What the studies show
item.description: Many people with arthritic knees cut back on walking to 'save' the joint. A surgeon reads a US cohort of 1,212 people with knee arthritis, a step-count study of 1,788 people and two reviews of exercise trials to see whether walking wears the knee out.

item.title: Do noisy, cracking knees mean arthritis is coming?
item.description: Grinding, cracking or popping when you squat or climb stairs worries a lot of people. A surgeon reads the 2025 meta-analysis of 103 studies on knee crepitus and two long-term US cohorts to see what the noise does, and does not, predict.

item.title: How long does a hip replacement really last?
item.description: Many people hear that a new hip wears out after 10 or 15 years. A surgeon reads the Lancet meta-analysis of more than 215,000 hip replacements in national registries and a UK study of 63,000 patients, including the less comfortable 25-year figure.

item.title: Are falls after 60 just part of ageing? What exercise does to your fall risk
item.description: Many people assume falls come with age and nothing can be done. A surgeon reads the Cochrane review of 108 randomised trials with over 23,000 older people — which exercises cut falls, which are uncertain, and what happens if you stop.

item.title: Do gel (hyaluronic acid) injections help knee arthritis?
item.description: Hyaluronic acid 'gel' or 'lubricant' injections are widely offered for knee arthritis. A surgeon reads the two largest meta-analyses of the placebo-controlled trials — 169 trials and over 21,000 people — and what they found about pain relief and side effects.

item.title: Does a torn ACL always need surgery? What the randomised trials found
item.description: An ACL tear is often assumed to mean a reconstruction. A surgeon reads the two randomised trials that compared early reconstruction with rehabilitation first (and surgery only if needed), and the Cochrane review that graded them.

item.title: Does a knee replacement only last 10–15 years?
item.description: Many people put off a knee replacement because they have heard it wears out after 10 or 15 years. A surgeon reads the Lancet registry meta-analysis of nearly 300,000 knees and a UK study of 54,000 patients on how long the implants last, and why age at surgery matters.

item.title: Do cortisone shots help knee arthritis — or wreck the knee?
item.description: Steroid injections are one of the most common treatments for an arthritic knee, and one of the most argued about. A surgeon reads the Cochrane review, the two-year injection trials and the large cohort studies on how long the relief lasts and what happens to the cartilage.

item.title: Does keyhole surgery help a worn-out knee? What the sham-surgery trials found
item.description: Arthroscopic 'clean-ups' and partial meniscectomy were among the most common knee operations for middle-aged and older adults. A surgeon reads the placebo-controlled trials, the head-to-head trials against exercise therapy, and the meta-analysis of benefits and harms.

item.title: Should you rest in bed when your back goes out?
item.description: Bed rest was standard advice for acute low back pain for decades. A surgeon reads the randomised trials and the Cochrane review on resting versus staying active — and what the evidence says to do instead.

item.title: Can your joints really predict the rain?
item.description: Many people with arthritis say they can feel a change in the weather. A surgeon reads the large studies on rain, cold, humidity and air pressure — and what they do and do not show about joint and back pain.

item.title: Your MRI shows a bulging disc. Is that why your back hurts?
item.description: Disc bulges and 'degeneration' are common on the scans of people with no back pain at all. A surgeon reads the evidence on what spine MRI findings do and do not explain — and when a scan helps.

item.title: Do lateral wedge insoles help knee pain from arthritis? What the placebo-controlled trials found
item.description: Lateral wedge insoles are meant to take load off the inner knee. When trials compared them with plain flat insoles, the pain benefit disappeared. A surgeon reads the evidence on insoles and knee braces.

item.title: Does creatine cause hair loss? The one study behind the fear — and the trial that tested it
item.description: The creatine-baldness worry traces back to a single 2009 study of rugby players. A surgeon reads it, and the 2025 randomised trial that finally measured hair.

item.title: Do cold plunges speed muscle recovery? What the meta-analyses show — and the catch for lifters
item.description: Ice baths are everywhere. A surgeon reads the meta-analyses: cold water eases soreness, does little for strength recovery, and done after every strength session may shrink your gains.

item.title: Is it too late to build muscle after 60? What the trials show
item.description: Many people believe lost muscle can't be rebuilt in later life. A surgeon reads the meta-analyses of strength training in adults over 50, over 75 and even over 90.

item.title: Does vitamin D prevent falls in older adults? What the trials found
item.description: Vitamin D is often recommended to keep older people on their feet. A surgeon reads the meta-analyses of falls trials — and the one trial where a big yearly dose made falls more common.

item.title: Do calcium supplements prevent fractures? What the trials found
item.description: Calcium pills are taken by millions of older adults to protect their bones. A surgeon reads the large trials and meta-analyses on calcium, vitamin D and broken bones.

item.title: Is sitting the new smoking? What the numbers actually show
item.description: Long sitting is linked to a higher risk of death, but the size of that link is far smaller than smoking's, and enough daily activity appeared to cancel it in a study of over a million people.

item.title: Is weight training bad for older joints? What the trials show
item.description: Many people over 50 avoid lifting weights to protect their knees. A surgeon reads three large bodies of evidence on strength training, joint pain and safety.

item.title: Do you really need 10,000 steps a day? What step-counter studies show
item.description: The benefits of walking rise steeply up to about 7,000 steps a day and then level off, especially after 60. A surgeon explains what two large analyses found.

item.title: Does stretching before exercise prevent injuries? Strength training does far more
item.description: A meta-analysis of 25 trials with 26,610 people found no injury-prevention effect from stretching, while strength training cut sports injuries to less than a third. A surgeon explains.

item.title: Does glucosamine rebuild knee cartilage? What the trials actually measured
item.description: Glucosamine is sold as a cartilage builder. Large trials that measured the joint space on X-rays found tiny or no differences from placebo. A surgeon explains the numbers.

item.title: Biotin for hair: does it work, and can it throw off your blood tests?
item.description: Biotin has helped hair only in people with a deficiency or an underlying condition. High doses can also distort lab tests — most often thyroid tests. A surgeon explains.

item.title: Collagen for joints and skin: what the best trials actually say
item.description: Pooled trials say collagen helps skin, but the independent, high-quality ones don't. For joints, the benefit is short-lived and the evidence weak. A surgeon reads the fine print.

item.title: Does cracking your knuckles cause arthritis?
item.description: One of the most repeated warnings in medicine has little evidence behind it. What the studies of habitual knuckle crackers found — and what the 'pop' actually is.

item.title: Does running ruin your knees? What 125,000 people tell us
item.description: Recreational runners had less hip and knee arthritis than non-runners in a large meta-analysis. Competitive runners had more. A surgeon explains what that does and does not prove.

item.title: Grip strength: the vital sign hiding in your hand
item.description: Weaker grip goes with shorter life in huge studies across the world. What that does and does not mean, and what you can actually change.
